```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)   # chunks that need your data; section 1's chunks set eval themselves
```

This page covers what to prepare and which options to consider when you run SigDoTS on a
real dataset. Section 1 runs on small objects built from the example data; the rest is shown
without running, because it needs your data. A complete run on a public Visium section
(human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, 151673) is the [real data application](dlpfc.html).

## 1. Input data: what `sigdots()` accepts

`sigdots()` takes the data in whichever of these forms you have:

| You have | Call | Where the pieces come from |
|---|---|---|
| a **Seurat** object (Visium, Xenium, Slide-seq, ... loaded with `Load10X_Spatial()` or similar) | `sigdots(obj, K0 = 10)` | the normalised `"data"` layer of the default assay; the variable genes from `FindVariableFeatures()`; the positions from the object's image or FOV |
| a **SpatialExperiment** object (Bioconductor: `read10xVisium()`, spatialLIBD, STexampleData, ...) | `sigdots(spe, K0 = 10, genes = hvg)` | the `"logcounts"` assay; the genes you name (all genes if there are at most 5,000); `spatialCoords(spe)` |
| a **SingleCellExperiment** without positions, or an AnnData file read with `zellkonverter::readH5AD()` | `sigdots(sce, coords = xy, K0 = 10)` | the `"logcounts"` assay; `coords` given by you |
| a **counts matrix** (genes x spots) and a coordinate table | `sigdots(sigdots_prepare(counts), xy, K0 = 10)` | `sigdots_prepare()` log-normalises and keeps the 2,000 most variable genes |
| an **expression matrix** you normalised yourself | `sigdots(x, xy, K0 = 10)` | `x`: one row per spot, one column per gene; `xy`: one row per spot, two columns, same order |

Whatever the form, two things end up inside: an expression matrix with one row per spot and
one column per gene, normalised and log-transformed, and the spots' positions (any unit;
SigDoTS measures distances in units of the typical distance between neighbouring spots).
`candidate_labels` can be the name of a metadata column of the object (for example a BANKSY or
Seurat clustering) instead of a vector.

The examples below build small objects from the package's example data, so that they run
here; with real data the objects come from the loading functions named in the table.

All three examples start from the same toy counts matrix, made from the example data:

```{r toy-counts, eval = TRUE}
library(SigDoTS)
counts <- Matrix::Matrix(t(round(expm1(sigdots_example$x) * 50)), sparse = TRUE)   # genes x spots
dim(counts)
```

### A Seurat object

```{r seurat, eval = requireNamespace("Seurat", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("SeuratObject", quietly = TRUE)}
library(Seurat)
# A toy Seurat object: the counts and the spot positions as a FOV. With real data:
# obj <- Load10X_Spatial("path/to/spaceranger/outs")
obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts, assay = "Spatial")
obj[["slice1"]] <- CreateFOV(CreateCentroids(data.frame(sigdots_example$coords, cell = colnames(counts))),
                             type = "centroids", assay = "Spatial")

obj <- NormalizeData(obj, verbose = FALSE)                       # the "data" layer SigDoTS uses
obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj, nfeatures = 150, verbose = FALSE)   # the genes SigDoTS uses

fit <- sigdots(obj, K0 = 5, verbose = FALSE)
fit
obj <- add_domains(obj, fit)       # adds obj$sigdots_domain and obj$sigdots_candidate_domain
table(obj$sigdots_domain, sigdots_example$region)
```

With a Seurat object you can also name the assay (`assay = "SCT"`), choose the genes
(`genes = VariableFeatures(obj)[1:1000]`), give the positions yourself (`coords = ...`), or
start from a clustering stored in the metadata (`candidate_labels = "seurat_clusters"`). Seurat
objects created with Seurat 4 (images of class `VisiumV1`) work the same way; their
coordinates are `imagecol` and `imagerow`, so `plot(fit)` may appear flipped vertically
relative to the tissue image (add `ggplot2::scale_y_reverse()`).

### A SpatialExperiment object

```{r spe, eval = requireNamespace("SpatialExperiment", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("scuttle", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("scran", quietly = TRUE)}
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(scuttle)
library(scran)
# A toy SpatialExperiment: with real data, spe <- read10xVisium("path/to/spaceranger/outs")
spe <- SpatialExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts), spatialCoords = sigdots_example$coords)

spe <- logNormCounts(spe)                                        # the "logcounts" assay SigDoTS uses
hvg <- getTopHVGs(modelGeneVar(spe), n = 150)                    # the genes SigDoTS uses

fit <- sigdots(spe, K0 = 5, genes = hvg, verbose = FALSE)
fit
spe <- add_domains(spe, fit)       # adds colData(spe)$sigdots_domain and $sigdots_candidate_domain
table(colData(spe)$sigdots_domain, sigdots_example$region)
```

For Visium data `spatialCoords(spe)` holds pixel positions (`pxl_col_in_fullres`,
`pxl_row_in_fullres`); any unit works. A `SingleCellExperiment` without positions, for
example from `zellkonverter::readH5AD()` on a Scanpy file, needs `coords = `; Scanpy keeps the
positions in `obsm["spatial"]`, which becomes `reducedDim(sce, "spatial")`.

### A counts matrix

```{r counts, eval = TRUE}
# counts: genes x spots, raw; xy: spots x 2, rows in the same order as the columns of counts
x <- sigdots_prepare(counts, n_genes = 150)   # log(1 + counts per 10,000), 150 most variable genes
dim(x)
fit <- sigdots(x, sigdots_example$coords, K0 = 5, verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

### Notes on the genes

Any normalisation and gene selection can be used; the examples take the most variable genes
because that is what the paper did. The genes enter two places: the principal components
used for the candidate domains and the tree, and the split statistic, which uses **all** the
genes given. Genes with larger variance weigh more in both; scale the columns first if you
want every gene to count equally. Give at least a few hundred genes; the simulated data need
a gene covariance to be estimated.

If an expression matrix has one row per gene, SigDoTS stops and tells you to use `t(x)`.

## 2. The candidate domains

SigDoTS starts from an over-segmentation and decides which of its candidate domains to merge.
It assumes that **each candidate domain lies inside one true domain**; it can merge candidate
domains, but it cannot split one.

**With the built-in clustering** give `K0`, the number of candidate domains, larger than the
number of domains you expect (twice as many is a reasonable start):

```r
fit <- sigdots(x, coords, K0 = 10)                                   # k-means (default)
fit <- sigdots(x, coords, K0 = 10, cluster_method = "banksy")        # needs Banksy
fit <- sigdots(x, coords, K0 = 10, cluster_method = "bayesspace")    # needs BayesSpace
```

BANKSY and BayesSpace are Bioconductor packages and are not installed with SigDoTS; if
they are missing, SigDoTS stops and prints the installation command. Arguments for them go
in `cluster_args`.

**With your own labels** (for example from Seurat, Scanpy or a BANKSY run you have already
tuned):

```r
fit <- sigdots(x, coords, candidate_labels = my_labels, cluster_method = "kmeans")
```

The tree is built from your labels. The simulated datasets, however, are still grouped
with `cluster_method`, because SigDoTS must apply a clustering procedure to them. The test
is therefore calibrated for labels made the way `cluster_method` makes them; when your
labels come from a very different method, keep this in mind when you read the p-values.

**Size of the parts.** Every tested part of the tree needs enough spots for the spatial
parameters to be estimated (on a regular grid, about 80 or more). With many small candidate
domains, the lower parts of the tree may be too small; SigDoTS then leaves them untested
and warns. A smaller `K0` avoids this.

**A region of interest.** SigDoTS can be run on any subset of spots, for example one
anatomical layer, to ask whether that layer has substructure. Subset `x` and `coords` to
the spots of the region and run as usual.

## 3. Exact or approximate spatial computation

The simulated datasets need the spots' spatial correlation matrix, an n x n matrix for a
part of the tree with n spots.

* `spatial_method = "vecchia"` (default): the Vecchia approximation with
  `vecchia_neighbors = 60` neighbours. Memory and time grow roughly linearly with n.
* `spatial_method = "exact"`: the exact matrix and its eigendecomposition. Memory grows
  with n^2 (about 16 GiB at 20,000 spots) and time faster still. SigDoTS stops before a
  test whose estimated memory exceeds `sigdots_control(max_exact_memory_gib = 16)`; raise
  it if your machine has more memory.

## 4. Run time, cores and memory

* `n_cores` runs the simulated datasets of a test in parallel (Linux and macOS; on Windows
  SigDoTS uses one core). The result is the same for any number of cores.
* The first test, on all spots, is the slowest; it uses 19 simulated datasets at
  `alpha = 0.05`.

Measured in the paper's scalability experiment (simulated data with 2,000 genes and three
domains, `K0 = 5`, exact spatial computation, 10 cores; mean of 2 datasets per size; peak
memory of the whole run including the 10 worker processes):

| Spots | Run time | Peak memory |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 400 | 14 s | 2.7 GiB |
| 900 | 32 s | 3.5 GiB |
| 1,600 | 2.0 min | 5.3 GiB |
| 2,500 | 4.3 min | 6.1 GiB |
| 5,041 | 9.2 min | 9.6 GiB |
| 10,000 | 18 min | 19.8 GiB |

With the default Vecchia approximation, 2,500 spots took a median of 4.0 minutes on
three-domain data and 1.4 minutes on one-domain data (10 cores, 680 datasets). At 50,176
spots the exact computation took 12 hours and 206 GiB; use Vecchia there.

Estimating the spatial parameters uses memory that grows with the square of the number of
spots in a part of the tree, whatever the spatial method: measured for one estimate with
200 genes, 0.31 GiB at 2,500 spots, 2.05 GiB at 10,000, 7.42 GiB at 19,881 and 28.99 GiB
at 40,000. For very large samples, run SigDoTS on a computer with enough memory, or on a
region of interest.

## 5. Options you will rarely change

`sigdots_control()` holds the remaining settings; the defaults are those used in the
paper. The most likely to matter:

* `ell_range = c(0.3, 40)`: the range of `ell` (in spot spacings) searched. If SigDoTS
  warns that `ell` is at the upper end, rerun with a wider range, for example
  `control = sigdots_control(ell_range = c(0.3, 80))`.
* `min_node_size = 20`, `min_child_size = 8`: parts or sides smaller than this are not
  tested.
* `B_cap = 5000`: the largest number of simulated datasets for one test. A test on very
  few of very many spots has a tiny level and may need more; SigDoTS then warns.

Other arguments of `sigdots()`: `alpha` (0.05), `B_min`, `B_max` (10 and 10), `n_pcs` (15),
`seed` (1), and `pvalue_method` (`"monte_carlo"`, or `"normal_adaptive"` for a normal
approximation of the p-value that needs fewer simulated datasets; see `?sigdots`).

## 6. Reading the result

`print(fit)`, `summary(fit)`, `domains(fit)` and `plot(fit, type = ...)` are explained in
`vignette("SigDoTS")`. `add_domains(object, fit)` writes
the domain of every spot into a Seurat or SpatialExperiment object; `domains(fit)` returns one
row per spot in the order of the data for anything else.

For a figure of the domains on the tissue with your own styling, take
`domains(fit)$domain` and the coordinates and draw them with ggplot2, or add layers to
`plot(fit)`, which is a ggplot object.
